questions.q: What fundamentally makes AI Data Attacks different from evasion attacks?
options: They only work on image models
They require physical access to the server
They corrupt the data or model the system is built on, not the live input
They only affect the user interface
questions.explanation: Data attacks undermine the model's foundation, its training data or stored file, while evasion attacks trick an already-deployed model at decision time.

questions.q: According to the module, what are the three main goals a data attacker typically aims for?
options: Degrade, target, and backdoor
Encrypt, compress, and delete
Scan, patch, and monitor
Train, test, and validate
questions.explanation: Data attackers generally aim for one of three outcomes: degrading overall performance, targeting one specific case, or hiding a secret trigger through a backdoor.

questions.q: In a label flipping attack, what does the attacker actually change?
options: The model's source code
The model's hyperparameters
The features (input data) of the samples
The labels (correct answers) attached to samples
questions.explanation: Label flipping leaves the features untouched and changes only the labels, for example relabeling a 'positive' review as 'negative'.

questions.q: What is the difference between random and targeted label flipping?
options: Random flipping only works on images; targeted flipping only works on text
Random flipping degrades overall accuracy; targeted flipping attacks only one specific class
There is no real difference between them
Targeted flipping requires physical access to the training server
questions.explanation: Random flipping simply makes the model less reliable overall, while targeted flipping surgically attacks a single class, such as relabeling only positive reviews as negative.

questions.q: Why are clean-label attacks harder to detect than label flipping?
options: They only run at midnight
They use encryption to hide the data
The labels stay correct and plausible, so label audits find nothing wrong
They delete the training data afterward
questions.explanation: Clean-label attacks modify features while keeping labels honest, so defenses that check labels miss them entirely. You must inspect the feature space instead.

questions.q: In a clean-label attack, whose data points does the attacker actually modify?
options: The target's own data points
Random points scattered across the entire dataset
Points belonging to a different class near the target, nudging them toward the decision boundary
Only the model's validation set
questions.explanation: The attacker shifts nearby points from another class toward the boundary while keeping their original labels, forcing the model to bend its boundary and misclassify the real target.

questions.q: What two metrics define a successful Trojan/backdoor attack?
options: Small file size and fast training
Low latency and high throughput
High memory usage and low CPU usage
High Clean Accuracy (stealth) and high Attack Success Rate (effectiveness)
questions.explanation: A good backdoor keeps Clean Accuracy high so it passes normal tests, while keeping Attack Success Rate high so the trigger reliably works when present.

questions.q: Why do backdoors often pass all normal model evaluation tests?
options: Evaluators never test image models
On clean, untriggered inputs the model behaves accurately and normally; only the trigger reveals the hidden behavior
Backdoors disable the evaluation process entirely
Backdoors only activate during training, never during testing
questions.explanation: Since the backdoor only activates when the specific trigger appears, standard testing on clean data shows nothing wrong, which is exactly what makes backdoors so dangerous.

questions.q: Why is loading a pickle-based model file from an untrusted source dangerous?
options: Pickle files are always corrupted
It changes your Python version
It can execute arbitrary attacker code automatically during loading
Pickle files are too large to open
questions.explanation: Pickle, and torch.load with weights_only=False, can run code embedded via __reduce__ the moment the file is loaded, turning a simple load into remote code execution.

questions.q: What is the recommended safe alternative to loading a model with plain pickle or weights_only=False?
options: Use safetensors and set weights_only=True
Load the model twice to verify it
Convert the model to a PDF first
Disable your antivirus before loading
questions.explanation: Safetensors stores only numeric data and cannot execute code, and weights_only=True in torch.load refuses to run arbitrary objects, both closing off the RCE risk.

questions.q: Why do attackers hide data in the least significant bits (LSBs) of model weights?
options: LSBs are encrypted by default
Only LSBs can hold text
LSBs store the model's accuracy
Changing LSBs barely alters the number, so the model still works and the change is hard to spot
questions.explanation: Flipping an LSB changes a float by a microscopic amount, so accuracy is preserved and the hidden payload stays statistically inconspicuous across millions of weights.

questions.q: How do pickle deserialization and tensor steganography combine into a full attack?
options: Steganography hides a payload in the weights, and the pickle vulnerability extracts and runs it on load
They are unrelated techniques that cannot be combined
Steganography encrypts the pickle file for extra security
Pickle deserialization deletes the hidden payload automatically
questions.explanation: The steganography hides the payload inside the weight tensor's LSBs, while a malicious __reduce__ method extracts and executes that payload the moment the file is loaded.

questions.q: How does 'package hallucination' (slopsquatting) become a security attack?
options: The AI deletes real packages
The AI encrypts the developer's code
An attacker registers the fake package names an AI keeps suggesting, then fills them with malware
Packages become too expensive to install
questions.explanation: AIs hallucinate non-existent package names consistently. Attackers register those exact names with malicious code, so developers who trust the AI's suggestion install malware.

questions.q: What makes hallucinated package names a reliable target for attackers?
options: AIs consistently suggest the same fake names repeatedly, giving attackers a predictable target
Package names are randomly generated each time
AIs only hallucinate once per day
Hallucinated names are always identical to real packages
questions.explanation: Because the same fake package name tends to get suggested repeatedly across sessions, attackers can reliably predict and register exactly the names developers are likely to install.

questions.q: What is the primary technique behind abuse detection evasion?
options: Deleting the detector's training data
Keeping the harmful meaning intact while changing the surface form enough to fool the detector
Overloading the detector with excessive requests
Bribing the detector's developers
questions.explanation: Evasion techniques like homoglyphs, spacing, and paraphrasing preserve the harmful meaning while changing the surface text just enough that the detector no longer recognizes it.

questions.q: Why does text normalization help defend against homoglyph-based evasion?
options: It deletes all Unicode characters from the input
It collapses lookalike Unicode characters back to a standard form before detection runs
It translates the text into a different language
It blocks all non-English input entirely
questions.explanation: Normalization, such as NFKC plus explicit homoglyph mapping, converts lookalike characters back to their standard ASCII form before the detector runs, closing the gap attackers exploit.

questions.q: What is the core principle behind a two-stage guardrail pipeline?
options: Retrain the model every hour
Filter both what goes into the model (input) and what comes out (output)
Only check the model's speed
Store all data in plain text
questions.explanation: Input guardrails block malicious requests before they reach the model, and output guardrails filter harmful or leaky responses before they reach the user.

questions.q: Why are guardrails alone not considered a complete security solution?
options: Guardrails only work on weekends
A determined attacker may bypass any single check, so layered defenses are needed
Guardrails are too expensive to maintain
Guardrails only protect against SQL injection
questions.explanation: Guardrails are one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy. No single check is foolproof, so they need to be combined with validation, monitoring, and least privilege.

questions.q: What does 'provenance' mean in the context of AI data security?
options: The model's accuracy score on a test set
The amount of storage a dataset consumes
Knowing and tracking the true source of every piece of data or model
The speed at which a model can be retrained
questions.explanation: Provenance means knowing exactly where every dataset, sample, or model file actually came from. Without it, tampering is far harder to trace and detect.

questions.q: According to the module's six pillars of AI data security, what does 'least privilege' specifically protect against?
options: Slow model inference times
A compromised account or system being able to cause more damage than necessary, such as freely editing training data
Running out of disk space
Users forgetting their passwords
questions.explanation: Least privilege limits what any single account or system component can do, so that even if it's compromised, the resulting damage, such as tampering with training data, stays contained.
